Known data defects

Written into protocol.json up front, so all three systems met the same data, and none could claim a lucky clean-up.

  • 2014A third of the year is simply missing: 64 days of ~310.
  • mid-2014A system migration changes the till code and the file format. Sales levels either side are not comparable.
  • 2020-06The shop starts opening on Mondays. The weekly shape changes mid-record.
  • 2021 onA second till appears that sells almost no bread, easy to double-count.
  • 95 daysThe same till was exported twice, usually one partial file and one complete one.
  • 2022Thin again, 92 days of ~310, which is why it is scored as a separate window.

What EDA found

Bread sold on every trading day, and its autocorrelation
The comb repeats every 6 lags, not 7. The shop closed Mondays for all but the last seven months of the record, so its week is six trading days long. That single number is why every seasonal model in the run carries period 6 — including SARIMA’s (0,1,1,6).
Written to state at iteration 1
  • 2,897 daystrading days from 2010-11-16 to 2020-12-31, after the store and product filters
  • ACF lag 6the dominant spike, not 7. Inherited by every seasonal model downstream
  • 2020-06-01regime change: the shop starts opening Mondays. Recorded once here, respected by Preprocess, FE and Training
  • ADF p = 0.0005stationary enough to model in levels, so no differencing was forced on the ML path
  • 50 zero daysdays the shop traded but sold no bread. The reason the metric below is MAE and not MAPE
  • MAEthe metric, chosen here and never revisited
  • 38.0 → 47.5a provisional naive MAE per horizon, superseded at iteration 4 by the Baseline skill’s real floor of 31.26–42.14
  • 2 sources cutthe second competitor file and all three delivery files: no path from either to a daily bread count
Annual mean — the level it has to track down
390 units in 2010, 273 in 2020. A 30% fall across the record, and the reason a year_trend feature exists at all.
Mean by day of week, ±1 sd
Sunday 416, Monday 241. Monday is the widest bar in the week (sd 93) on the thinnest evidence: it exists on 31 of the 2,897 days, every one of them after June 2020.
Distribution on days the shop traded
Mean 321, near-symmetric, with a thin right tail past 500. No skew correction and no log transform were warranted, and none was applied.

Data splits

Test: 2021 withheld
2,027 scored pairs
362 dates, 6 horizons, 11 with zero sales
Test: stress withheld
416 scored pairs

Why cut it this way
  • On date, never at random. Adjacent days are near-duplicates: a random split hands the model the answer.
  • Routing only, no cleaning. Nothing decided with the test rows in view can reach the training rows.
  • Two test windows, scored apart. 2021 is an ordinary year; 2022–23 is thin and post-shock.
The internal split, plotted by Preprocess

Two things this picture gives away for free: the 2014–15 hole in the record, and the falling level that the validation window sits inside, and that the holdout, further right and off this chart, sits even further down.

And the 46 it was never given
  • 18 anchorsthe naive baseline’s own per-horizon forecasts. The single heaviest block in the agentic model, worth +3.37 MAE on its own
  • 8 lags1, 2, 3, 7, 14, 35, 63, 91 days back, each looked up by calendar date. FLAML sees one row at a time and has no notion of yesterday
  • 11 calendarBelgian public holidays, Flemish school breaks, Gentse Feesten, days-to-next-holiday. All of it came from Domain Research, which AutoML has no equivalent of
  • 3 regime flagsthe Monday closure, the 7/7 switch, the 2014 gap. Nothing tells FLAML the series changed shape mid-record
  • ratio targetsfour of six agentic champions predict a ratio to an anchor rather than units. Choosing a target form is not something a search over hyperparameters can do

This is the whole argument in one card: the gap is not model choice. Both systems land on gradient-boosted trees. The gap is that one of them read the data first.

Worth saying out loud

Given the same rows and more than twice the time, AutoML closes most of the gap: 64.7 → 52.6. It still loses to the agentic pipeline by 6 units pooled, and it still wins outright at t+90. The fair number to argue against is 52.6, not 64.7.

Where the agent was wrong

iteration 12 The anchor was reading the wrong weekday
  • wrongthe naive anchors took the same weekday as the origin date, not the target date. At any horizon that is not a multiple of 7 those are different days — so the model’s single heaviest feature was anchored to the wrong day of the week.
  • caughtby Diagnosis, on the gap between what the anchor scored and the floor it was supposed to represent.
  • fixedfor origin D, target_dow = DOW(D + h). Median of the last W values on that weekday, all strictly before D. Rebuilt at h = 1, 30, 60, 90.
h+1 anchor, validation MAE54.4131.40
iteration 20 It had left the loss on the default
  • wrongLightGBM ran on its default squared-error objective while the target was a ratio. In the agent’s own words: “MSE is pulled toward post-COVID outlier ratios, causing fold-3 failure.”
  • caughtby the fold-3 collapse itself, once multi-fold evaluation was in place. A single validation split would have hidden it.
  • fixedobjective = regression_l1 on every model from here on — and written into the handoff as a durable rule, so clearing the context could not quietly undo it.
h+1 after the fixMSEregression_l1beats its floor on all 3 folds
iteration 22 It was comparing two different row sets
  • wrongh = 60 was scored on 35 validation-origin rows, then measured against a floor of 40.04 computed on 95 validation-target dates. Two different row sets, one verdict — and the verdict was that the model had failed.
  • caughtby the agent re-reading its own floor definition two iterations later and noticing the schemes did not match.
  • fixedboth target forms retrained and re-scored on the correct 95-row scheme, and the scheme itself pinned as a durable rule.
h+60 vs a floor of 40.0445.2236.23the model was fine; the ruler was not
iterations 5 → 19 Its own relevance test threw away good features
  • wrongat iteration 5 a Spearman screen dropped five calendar features for near-zero correlation — is_official_public_holiday at r = −0.003, days_since_last_holiday at r = 0.004. A rank correlation between a daily count and a flag that fires on 65 days out of 2,897 is close to meaningless. It said drop.
  • caughtat iteration 19, when the agent went back through the Domain Research output hunting for evidence it had never used.
  • fixed11 features re-added, after first checking the periods actually land in the validation window: herfstvakantie 7 rows, kerstvakantie 11, official holidays 3.
the calendar block, on the holdout+1.16 MAEthe filter was wrong, not the features

Training skill

skills/training-skill/training.md 856 lines · scroll to read
nametraining-agent-skill
descriptionTrains a model on the feature-engineered dataset, evaluates it on the validation set, and produces the artifacts (trained model, metrics, feature importance, residuals) that Diagnosis needs to decide whether to loop back or accept the result. Every number it reports is a validation number; the unbiased held-out score is produced outside this pipeline after the run ends.

Training Skill

Purpose

Given the current feature set and a model family recommendation from context, fit a model on the training split, evaluate it on the validation split, and surface the diagnostics Diagnosis needs to reason about: metrics, feature importance, and residual patterns. This is the step that produces a concrete number for the Planner and a concrete residual signal for Diagnosis — not the final answer (that is end_model) but the best current answer given the feature set at hand.

Reference material

This skill has a references/ directory (general ML model-selection/tuning/evaluation knowledge, built from scikit-learn docs and vetted blog sources) and shares a shared-references/ directory with Preprocess/FE (model-specific data-readiness requirements). Consult these instead of re-deriving general ML knowledge inline — the procedure below points to the relevant section at each step:

-../baseline-skill/baseline.md — required at step 6a (mode == "baseline"). The closed six-rule menu that sets baseline_floor, and the five rules that keep the floor honest. Cheap to load and cheap to run; a wrong floor invalidates every later number in the run
-references/index.md — routing index for everything below
-references/model_selection_supervised.md — full classical-ML decision framework (linear, SVM, KNN, trees, ensembles, Naive Bayes, SGD, LDA/QDA, kernel approximation) — broader than the narrowed GBT/RF/Linear table this skill uses in step 2b
-references/model_selection_timeseries.md — classical statistical forecasting (ARIMA/SARIMA/ exponential smoothing family) vs. the ML-as-regression-on-lag-features path this skill defaults to
-references/cross_validation.md — CV strategy selection, including why time-series data needs TimeSeriesSplit/walk-forward validation instead of random k-fold
-references/hyperparameter_tuning.md — search method comparison (grid/random/successive halving/Bayesian optimization), typical hyperparameter ranges, and (§5) time-series-specific tuning notes
-references/evaluation_metrics.md — metric-selection framework (including MASE) and validation/learning-curve interpretation for diagnosing over/underfitting
-references/plotting_guide.md — condition → plot table covering when to generate each diagnostic beyond the fixed floor in step 14, with the insight/interpretation each one needs
-../shared-references/preprocessing_and_feature_engineering.md — model-specific scaling, encoding, and missing-value requirements, owned jointly with Preprocess; consult before assuming a feature is training-ready

Inputs

-dataset_path — the feature-engineered dataset. Must contain a _split column with values train and validation only. If a test value appears, stop and raise it as an issues entry — the genuinely held-out data was removed before this run began, so a partition named test here means something upstream invented one, and any metric quoted against it would be mistaken for a final number.
-target_column — the column to predict.
-task_type — one of regression, binary_classification, or multiclass_classification. Should be established by EDA and carried forward; Training does not re-derive it.
-feature_subset — the specific feature columns to use this call. Must not include target_column, date/timestamp columns, or _split. When the FE prediction-time availability audit flagged concurrent features, feature_subset should reflect whichever deployment scenario applies (see step 4).
-deployment_scenario — one of:
-retrospective — the model explains past demand using all available features including same-period concurrent measurements. Concurrent features may be included in feature_subset.
-live_forecast — the model will be used to predict a future period before it occurs. Concurrent features must be excluded from feature_subset; only pre_period features apply.
-unspecified — the deployment scenario has not been confirmed. Training proceeds with the full feature set but records a clarification_needed entry.
-context — prior reasoning from any upstream node: EDA recommended_strategy, Diagnosis hypothesis, Training observation from a prior iteration, or a direct Planner instruction. Always record which node and iteration each piece of context came from.
-mode — one of:
-baseline — the first Training call of every run. Fits no learned model: it scores the trivial baseline on the real train/validation split and establishes the floor every later iteration is measured against. See step 6a.
-initial — first *learned* model this run.
-incremental — re-train with a changed feature set, different hyperparameters, or a Diagnosis-driven modification. Loads the prior model path from state/current.json for comparison.
-rebuild — discard the prior model entirely and start fresh (e.g. model family change).
-mode_reasoning — why this mode was chosen.
-prior_model_path — path to the previously saved model (used in incremental mode for comparison; null in initial or rebuild). On a multi-horizon task this is a dict keyed by horizon; only the horizons being retrained this call need an entry.
-target_horizons — optional. A subset of context.forecast_horizons specifying which horizons to train this call. When absent or null, all horizons in context.forecast_horizons are trained. When present, only the listed horizons are fitted — all others are left as-is in state/current.json. This allows the Planner to loop on a single underperforming horizon without discarding the other horizons' already-validated models. The horizons listed must be a subset of context.forecast_horizons; an unlisted value is a blocking issues entry.
-iteration — the global iteration number, used to build every output path.

Tools available

-Code execution sandbox with pandas, numpy, scikit-learn, lightgbm, xgboost, optuna or sklearn.model_selection (for hyperparameter search), joblib (for model persistence)
-Plotting library for artifact generation — same "numbers, not images" rule: every plot gets a paired CSV of the values plotted
-File write access to artifacts/training/, data/, history/, code/, and reports/
-Read-only access to state/current.json and any file under history/

Procedure

Every step below is a floor, not a ceiling. If an additional check, technique, or diagnostic beyond what's specified here would genuinely help for this specific dataset and model family, pursue it. Record anything beyond the prescribed procedure in agent_initiated_findings with the same reasoning and confidence discipline used throughout.

0.Resolve the horizon set before anything else.

Read context.target_horizons if present; otherwise read context.forecast_horizons. This is the set of horizons this call trains — call it active_horizons. Record it in the output as horizons_trained_this_call. When target_horizons was used, also record horizons_skipped_this_call — the horizons in forecast_horizons that are not being retrained — so the Planner and Diagnosis can see exactly which models were touched.

When active_horizons holds more than one value, this call trains one model per active horizon — not one model scored at several lead times. Each horizon gets its own fit, on its own target column (<target>_h<h>, built by Feature Engineering), using its own feature subset (horizon_feature_subsets[h], which filters on all bounds — it excludes every feature whose min_horizon exceeds h, every feature whose max_horizon is below h (the naive predictors, each of which is correct only at its own horizon), and every feature whose known_future_horizon is below h — and marks each remaining feature evaluated_at: origin | target_date), its own hyperparameters, and its own artifact: iteration_<NNN>_training_model_h<h>.pkl.

The reason is not tidiness. A single model pooled across horizons learns mostly from the short ones — they dominate the sample and they are easier — and the long horizons inherit a fit built on features they will not have at their own origin. The per-horizon models can also legitimately differ: a lag-heavy model at h = 1 and a level-and-calendar model at h = 30 is the correct outcome, not an inconsistency to be smoothed away. Record each horizon's model family and hyperparameters separately, and never report a metric pooled across horizons without the per-horizon breakdown beside it.

Every step below then runs per active horizon. Where a decision is genuinely shared — the primary metric, the deployment scenario — record it once and say it applies to all; where it differs, record it per horizon. mode == "baseline" follows the same rule: the floor is scored per horizon, because the naive error grows with lead time and one pooled floor would be wrong at both ends. On a baseline call, target_horizons must not be used — the floor must be established for every horizon at once so it is never missing when a later call needs it.

A single-horizon task — forecast_horizons absent, or one value — runs exactly as before.

1.Resolve dataset and validate split integrity. Load dataset_path, verify _split column exists with the expected three values. Count rows per split and confirm none is empty. Verify target_column is present and has no NaN values in train or validation rows. Verify no column in feature_subset is the target or leaks it (sanity-check: no feature in feature_subset should have Spearman correlation > 0.98 with the target on the training set — flag any that do as suspected leakage and record in issues).

The naive predictors are the one expected exception to that 0.98 check. A short-horizon naive predictor is a near-copy of the target by design — that is what makes it a strong feature — and it is strictly causal, computed at origin target − h, which is the property the check is actually screening for. When the column is in context.protected_features and its max_horizon equals the horizon being trained, record the correlation as expected rather than as suspected leakage, and do not remove it. When it is not protected, or its max_horizon does not match, the flag stands and is a real finding: a naive predictor showing up in the wrong horizon's subset is exactly the leak this check catches.

In incremental mode, confirm feature_subset matches what's actually in the file.

2.Read context and select the specific model class to train.

2a. Check for an override first. If context contains an explicit model class from a Planner instruction or a Diagnosis hypothesis (e.g. "switch to XGBoost", "try Ridge as a baseline"), use it directly and skip the decision table below. Document the override source.

2b. Apply the model selection decision table. When no override exists, derive the model class from observable dataset properties already measured by EDA and Preprocess. Work through the table in order — earlier rows take precedence when multiple conditions apply. Record every property that fired and why, not just the final choice.

This table is a narrowed decision table specific to this pipeline's three supported families (gradient boosted trees, random forest, linear). For the full classical-ML decision space — SVM, KNN, Naive Bayes, discriminant analysis, kernel approximation, or whenever none of the rows below clearly fire — consult references/model_selection_supervised.md. For whether this GBT/RF/Linear-on-engineered-features approach is the right approach at all versus a classical statistical forecasting model (ARIMA/SARIMA/exponential smoothing), consult references/model_selection_timeseries.md §1 — this pipeline defaults to the "ML-as-regression on engineered features" path documented there, and that file's XGBoost/gradient-boosting note confirms the choice.

Dataset property (from EDA / Preprocess / FE context)Implication
n_train < 500Avoid GBT — overfits easily on small data. Prefer Ridge (regression) or shallow Random Forest (max_depth ≤ 5)
n_train 500–5000GBT is appropriate with moderate regularisation (lower learning rate, min_child_samples > 10)
n_train > 5000Full GBT or neural network if feature complexity warrants it
NaN values remain in any feature after preprocessingChoose LightGBM — it handles NaN natively without imputation. Classic scikit-learn trees require NaN-free input; see ../shared-references/preprocessing_and_feature_engineering.md §6 for the full model-by-model breakdown, including an open question about XGBoost's NaN handling worth resolving before treating this row as settled
Mixed feature types (OHE categoricals + numeric + sparse)Tree-based over linear — linear models need careful scaling and encoding to handle this mix; trees split on raw values. See ../shared-references/preprocessing_and_feature_engineering.md §§1–2 for the full scaling/encoding requirements by model family
Confirmed strong linear relationship with target (EDA R² > 0.7 from a linear fit, or target is near-Gaussian)Consider Ridge/Lasso as a competitor alongside tree-based; a linear model that performs similarly is strictly preferable for interpretability
Target has confirmed trend + seasonality (time-series task)Tree-based preferred — can learn non-linear seasonal interactions. Linear models need manual interaction terms to achieve comparable accuracy
n_features > 200 after encodingLightGBM over XGBoost — LightGBM's histogram-based algorithm scales better with high feature count
Target distribution is heavily right-skewed (skew > 3)Consider Tweedie or Poisson loss for count/rate targets (GBT supports this via objective parameter); or log-transform of the target (see step 6 sub-step)
Binary classification with class imbalance (minority class < 20%)GBT with scale_pos_weight (XGBoost) or class_weight="balanced" (LightGBM); record the imbalance ratio
Hard interpretability requirement stated in goalLogistic Regression, Ridge, or single Decision Tree (depth ≤ 4); do not use GBT if interpretability is non-negotiable

Specific class mapping from family to library:

-gradient_boosted_trees + NaN features present → LGBMRegressor / LGBMClassifier
-gradient_boosted_trees + no NaN → LGBMRegressor / LGBMClassifier (preferred for speed) or XGBRegressor / XGBClassifier
-random_forest → sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestRegressor / RandomForestClassifier
-linear → sklearn.linear_model.Ridge (regression) / LogisticRegression (classification)

Record model_class (the exact library class name), model_family (the broad family), and model_selection_reasoning (which table rows fired and why) in the output.

2b-ts. Time-series tasks: name this fit's approach, and check the other one has a run. references/model_selection_timeseries.md §1 names three approaches. Two of them are non-automatic — classical statistical forecasting (ARIMA/SARIMA/SARIMAX/exponential smoothing, fitted to the time-ordered series itself) and ML-as-regression on engineered features (the GBT/RF/linear path of the table above, fed lag/rolling/calendar features). The third — Auto ARIMA, Prophet, an AutoML forecasting framework — is automatic and counts as neither.

Record ts_approach in the output on every time-series call: classical_statistical, ml_as_regression, or automatic.

Both non-automatic approaches must have been fitted at least once before the run may stop. Defaulting to ml_as_regression on every iteration and never fitting a classical model is not an acceptable run: the two put the structure in different places — one in the series' own autoregressive and seasonal terms, the other in engineered features — and which one this series rewards is an empirical question that only a fit answers. It is not settled by the decision table above, which already assumes the ML-as-regression framing.

Read context.ts_approaches_tried, which the Planner carries forward. If this call fits an approach that is already covered while the other has never been tried, fit what context asked for, then set ts_approach_gap in the output to the missing approach and note it in agent_initiated_findings — that is the field the Planner's coverage check and Diagnosis read.

The classical slot is filled by the ARIMA family, and plain ARIMA is fitted at least once. Exponential smoothing (SES, Holt-Winters) is a legitimate classical model and may be run in addition, but on its own it does not close the classical slot. The slot is closed by a fit from references/model_selection_timeseries.md §2's ARIMA family — ARIMA, SARIMA, or SARIMAX — chosen by that section's decision shortcut against what the series actually has (trend only → ARIMA; trend + seasonality → SARIMA; external regressors on top → SARIMAX).

When the shortcut sends you past plain ARIMA to SARIMA or SARIMAX, fit plain ARIMA anyway, once, alongside it. It is a cheap ablation and it answers a question the seasonal fit cannot: what the seasonal (or exogenous) terms are actually worth on this series. Report both numbers. Record which member of the family closed the slot in model_class, and record the plain-ARIMA comparison in agent_initiated_findings when ARIMA was not itself the chosen member.

Order selection (p,d,q) — and (P,D,Q)m where seasonal — follows references/hyperparameter_tuning.md §§1–2 and its classical-model row: search the orders, do not guess them, and do not leave d at a default. Establish d from a stationarity check (ADF plus the rolling mean/std plot in references/plotting_guide.md) and record the value with its evidence. An Auto ARIMA search may be used *to propose* orders, but the fit that closes the slot is the explicit one whose orders are recorded — the automatic approach still counts as automatic.

On a multi-horizon task, both approaches are fitted per horizon. A classical ARIMA-family fit is naturally per-horizon anyway (its forecast function is evaluated at each lead time from the same origin); the ML-as-regression path needs one model per horizon per step 0. The comparison between the two approaches is then made at each horizon, and it is allowed to come out differently at different lead times — classical winning at h = 30 while ML-as-regression wins at h = 1 is a real and common result, and reporting only the pooled winner would hide it.

The comparison only means something if the split and the metric match. A classical fit is evaluated on the *same* validation rows with the *same* primary metric as the ML-as-regression fits. That a classical model cannot consume the engineered feature set is expected — it is the substance of the comparison, not a defect — but a different split or a different metric makes the two numbers unreadable next to each other.

2c. Extract metric configuration from context.

-Primary metric — from EDA's recommended_metric or a Diagnosis override. If unspecified, default to MAE for regression, F1 for binary classification, macro-F1 for multiclass. Always document why this metric was chosen or defaulted. These are this pipeline's fixed defaults — see references/evaluation_metrics.md for the full decision framework (e.g. when Balanced Accuracy, F-beta, ROC AUC, or Pinball loss would be preferable) if Diagnosis or the Planner questions a default.
-Secondary metrics — one or more supplementary metrics. For time-series regression, always include MASE (see step 7). For classification, always include AUC-ROC.
-Feature-selection posture — whether to include all features in feature_subset or apply any last-minute pruning before fitting.
3.Resolve feature subset per deployment_scenario. If deployment_scenario == "live_forecast": confirm no concurrent feature from the FE prediction-time audit is in feature_subset. Remove any that are and log the removal. If deployment_scenario == "retrospective": all features in feature_subset are permitted. If deployment_scenario == "unspecified": proceed with the full feature_subset and raise a non-blocking clarification_needed entry asking the Planner to confirm the scenario. Note in the report that metrics are computed on the concurrent-included feature set.

Never prune a protected feature out of feature_subset. Every column in context.protected_features whose max_horizon matches the horizon being trained stays in, whatever the feature-selection posture says and whatever a last-minute pruning step would otherwise do. If this call has evidence that one should go, fit with it anyway and raise a blocking clarification_needed naming the column and the evidence — the user decides, per the Planner's Clarification Handling section. Leaving a horizon's own naive predictor out is not a pruning decision this node gets to make.

A protected feature is still subject to horizon scoping: naive_h7_* is absent from the h = 30 subset because it is only correct at h = 7, not because anything was pruned.

4.Pre-training integrity checks. Before fitting anything:
-Confirm the training split is strictly earlier than the validation split (for time-series tasks). If rows overlap in time, record a blocking issues entry and stop.
-Confirm no NaN values remain in any column in feature_subset for training or validation rows. If NaN exists, record in issues — do not silently drop rows or impute here (that is Preprocess's job; either request a Preprocess fix or fail the call).
-Check rows-to-features ratio on the training set (n_train_rows / n_features). If below 10×, record a warning in issues — proceed but flag the risk.
5.Configure model and hyperparameter strategy. Choose one of:
-Use defaults (mode == "initial" with no prior search results): set sensible defaults for the chosen model family (e.g. for gradient boosted trees: n_estimators=500, max_depth=5, learning_rate=0.05, subsample=0.8, colsample_bytree=0.8). Document each default and the reasoning.
-Lightweight search (Diagnosis suggested a hyperparameter hypothesis, or mode == "incremental" with a search instruction): use TimeSeriesSplit (not random k-fold — see Guardrails) with 3–5 folds over the training set only. Evaluate on the fold's held-out portion using the primary metric. Never let any fold's validation rows overlap with the global validation split. See references/hyperparameter_tuning.md §§1–2 for the full grid/random/halving/Bayesian-optimization comparison if a different search strategy is warranted, and §5 specifically for time-series tuning — walk-forward validation during search (not just final evaluation), and treating the lag/rolling window size itself as a tunable choice rather than a fixed guess.
-Accept explicit hyperparameters (Planner or Diagnosis passed specific values in context): use them directly and document the source.

For all strategies: document every hyperparameter used and the reasoning for its value or the search range. A hyperparameter left at its library default without documentation is an unrecorded assumption.

6.Train the model on _split == "train" rows only. Fit using only the resolved feature_subset columns and target_column. Record training time. After fitting, save the model to artifacts/training/iteration_<NNN>_training_model.pkl using joblib.dump.

6a. Baseline sub-step. Two different things are called a baseline here and the difference matters:

The floor (mode == "baseline", the run's first Training call). Follow ../baseline-skill/baseline.md — it is the whole procedure for this sub-step and is deliberately small: six trivial rules, one pass, no tuning. Do not hand-roll a single rule here. It scores the *trivial* predictors on the real split and reports the strongest as the floor, which is the part a hand-rolled version gets wrong: a lone seasonal naive (ŷ_t = y_{t-P}) is usually not the strongest trivial rule, and adopting it unchallenged sets the floor too low for the rest of the run. For plain regression the floor is the training mean, for classification the majority class, and the skill's rules on origin discipline and row alignment still apply. Compute the full metric set on it — for a time series that means MAE, RMSE and SMAPE (MASE against itself is 1.0 by construction; record it anyway so the tables line up) — and compute it per segment the goal is stated over, per horizon for a multi-horizon forecast. Write it to baseline_floor, then run the skill's Part B and write naive_predictor_features — the per-horizon naive predictor specs, selected on train rows only, that the next feature_engineering call materialises as protected columns. Both blocks go in the handoff in full, with formulas and parameters, because FE reimplements each one and cannot do that from a name. Then stop: this call trains nothing, saves no .pkl, and takes an iteration number like any other node.

Part B is not optional and not deferrable. It is the only point in the run where the naive predictors get selected, and Feature Engineering runs next. A baseline call that returns a floor without them leaves the run's feature sets permanently missing the one predictor class selected specifically for each horizon, and nothing downstream reports the absence.

This is the number the rest of the run exists to beat, and it is established first precisely so that no later iteration can quietly redefine what "good" means. EDA's trivial_baseline is the provisional version of it; this one is authoritative because it uses the same rows, the same metric and the same segments as every model that follows.

The reference model (mode == "initial"). When the first *learned* model is fitted, also fit a simple reference model on the same training rows immediately after it. This is a different question from the floor: it asks whether the primary model's complexity is earning its keep against something cheap but non-trivial. Repeat it in later iterations only when Diagnosis explicitly requests a re-comparison.

Choose the reference type from the table below:

Task typeBaseline
Time-series regressionRidge from sklearn.linear_model, fit on [time_index, <strongest_lag_feature>] only (two features maximum). If time_index does not exist, use the single highest-importance lag feature. Compute predictions on both train and val.
Plain regression (non-time-series)Mean predictor: always predicts the train-set mean of target_column.
Binary classificationMajority-class predictor: always predicts the most-frequent class in training.
Multiclass classificationMajority-class predictor.

Record the reference model's train and validation primary metric values in baseline_model. Neither the floor nor the reference model is saved as a .pkl artifact — both exist only for metric comparison. Do not compute feature importance or residuals for either. If the primary model's validation metric is worse than the reference model's, raise this as a high-confidence agent_initiated_finding — it almost always means a structural problem with the feature set or target leakage.

Every Training call reports its standing against the floor. Read context.baseline_floor and record vs_baseline_floor: the margin per segment and per horizon, not just pooled, and whether the model beats the floor everywhere or only on average. A model that wins pooled while losing on a third of the segments is the specific failure the per-segment floor exists to catch — the aggregate will never say so on its own.

6b. Target log-transform check. If EDA reported target skewness > 3 (or if the decision table in step 2b flagged it), apply np.log1p to target_column for the training fit and invert with np.expm1 before computing metrics. Document the transform in the output under training_summary.target_transform. Do not transform the target without recording it — an unrecorded transform makes Diagnosis's residual interpretation wrong. (Log transformation as a target-skew fix is also documented in ../shared-references/preprocessing_and_feature_engineering.md §5.2 alongside differencing, for consistency with how Preprocess/FE handle skew and non-stationarity elsewhere in the pipeline.)

7.Evaluate on _split == "validation" rows. Compute the primary metric and all secondary metrics on both train and validation sets (train metrics help assess overfitting in step 8). For each metric record both the value and the computation method.

Metric selection. This pipeline's fixed defaults per task type:

Task typePrimary (default)Secondary (always include)
RegressionMAERMSE, R², MAPE
Time-series regressionChosen by the agent from EDA's recommended_metric — MAE unless the goal argues otherwiseMAE, RMSE, SMAPE and MASE, always, whichever of them is not the primary — plus anything else the agent judges relevant
Binary classificationF1AUC-ROC, precision, recall, confusion matrix
Multiclass classificationMacro-F1Per-class F1, weighted-F1, confusion matrix

See references/evaluation_metrics.md §§2–4 for the full reasoning behind each of these (why MAE vs. RMSE vs. MAPE, why AUC-ROC pairs with F1, why MASE for time series) and for metrics to reach for outside these defaults (e.g. Balanced Accuracy under severe imbalance, Pinball loss for quantile targets). Report threshold used for classification (default 0.5); note if class imbalance is present. Flag MAPE if the target has near-zero values (division instability) — this is exactly why MASE is mandatory for time-series regression instead.

The time-series floor is four metrics, and it is not negotiable. On any time-series task, compute MAE, RMSE, SMAPE and MASE on both train and validation, every call, regardless of which one is primary. They are there because each answers a question the others cannot: MAE gives the typical error in the target's own units; RMSE weights the rare large miss, so the RMSE/MAE ratio says whether the error is spread evenly or concentrated in a few bad days; SMAPE is scale-free, so it is the only one of the four that compares honestly across segments, series or horizons of different magnitude; MASE prices the model against the seasonal naive.

Choosing the primary metric is still the agent's call — take EDA's recommended_metric, or depart from it with recorded reasoning, and add any further metric the task warrants. What this floor removes is the option of *not computing* one of the four, which is how a run ends up unable to answer "was that a uniformly small error or three catastrophic days?" after the fact.

When the four disagree, that disagreement is a finding, not noise. If RMSE ranks two iterations differently from MAE, the difference is outlier-driven and belongs in the report and in the handoff to Diagnosis — do not report only the primary metric's verdict and leave the contradiction unmentioned.

SMAPE and zeros: SMAPE is undefined where actual and predicted are both zero, and unstable where the actual is zero (closed days, stock-outs, off-season). State the convention used — excluding those rows, or defining 0/0 = 0 — record how many rows it affected, and never let the choice go unrecorded, because the two conventions can differ by several points on a series with many zero days.

MASE sub-step (time-series regression only): See references/evaluation_metrics.md §4 for the MASE formula and seasonal-naive-baseline procedure. This pipeline's specific requirement: compute the naive baseline MAE on the training set only — fit the denominator on train, apply it to normalise both train and val MAE (see Guardrails — this is the same leakage principle as fitting a scaler on train only). Record the seasonal period P used, the naive baseline MAE (train), and the resulting MASE for both train and validation.

8.Overfitting assessment. Compute the ratio of validation primary metric to train primary metric. For error metrics (MAE, RMSE, log-loss): ratio = val / train (> 1 means worse on val). For score metrics (R², AUC, F1): ratio = train / val (> 1 means worse on val). Classify:
RatioAssessment
< 1.05good_fit — negligible gap
1.05 – 1.25mild_overfit — monitor; may resolve with more data or lighter regularisation
1.25 – 2.0moderate_overfit — worth addressing; Diagnosis should investigate feature count or regularisation
> 2.0severe_overfit — likely cause: too many features relative to training rows, or data leakage

Also flag underfitting when validation metric is poor AND train metric is similarly poor (both far from a reasonable baseline), which suggests the model family or feature set is insufficient regardless of overfitting. When this ratio-based read is ambiguous or Diagnosis wants more than a single-number verdict, pair it with a validation/learning curve — see references/evaluation_metrics.md §6 for how to read those.

8b. Achievable-range check — required for every regression model, and a hard gate for tree-based ones. Overfitting is not the only way a model can be wrong in a way the primary metric hides. A tree ensemble predicts an average of training-set leaf values, so it can never output a value outside the range of the target it was trained on. If the series moves out of that range — a declining trend, a level shift, a regime change — the model cannot follow it, and no amount of tuning will fix it because the failure is in the target representation, not the hyperparameters.

Compute and record, on the validation rows:

   pred_min, pred_max                     the model's achievable output range
   y_min, y_max                           the actual range it is being asked to reach
   out_of_range_pct    = share of actual values outside [pred_min, pred_max]
   one_sided_bias_pct  = share of residuals sharing a sign
ReadingAssessmentWhat it means
out_of_range_pct < 1% and one_sided_bias_pct < 65%range_okthe model can reach where the data goes
out_of_range_pct 1–5%, or one_sided_bias_pct 65–80%range_warningrecord it, hand it to Diagnosis by name
out_of_range_pct > 5%, or one_sided_bias_pct > 80%range_failurethe model is mis-specified. Do not present it as a candidate without saying so

On range_failure with a tree-based model, the fix is a target representation change, not a hyperparameter change — see featureengineering.md step 2b. Say so explicitly in issues and in the handoff, and name the anchor the model already has available. A recalibration or bias-correction proposal is a *downstream* remedy for this and must not be offered as the primary one: it treats the symptom in the serving layer while the model stays unable to represent the level.

Watch for this being invisible on validation. These figures are computed on validation because that is the only partition Training may touch — but the defect they detect only appears once the target moves outside the training range. If Preprocess reported a larger drifting series and warned that validation sits closer to train than the unseen holdout will (split_info.holdout_representativeness, see preprocess.md step 3), then validation *understates* this failure and a range_ok here is not evidence of safety. Record that caveat alongside the numbers rather than letting a clean validation read stand unqualified.

Record all four numbers plus the assessment under overfitting_check as achievable_range. Plot the predicted-vs-actual range comparison when the assessment is anything other than range_ok — a histogram of actuals with the achievable range shaded is enough, and it makes the failure obvious to a reader who would skim past the numbers.

9.Extract and rank feature importance — by group, per ../shared-references/feature_attribution.md. That file is the specification; this step is the summary of what it requires.

Feature importance is not identifiable when features are correlated, so the reported value is grouped permutation importance on the validation set (never on train — permutation importance on train inflates the importance of memorised features):

a. Cluster features by Spearman rank correlation, merging at |rho| >= 0.6. Record the clusters — "these features are the same variable" is itself a finding. b. Permute every column in a cluster together with the same row permutation, re-score the final prediction, and record the MAE increase over >= 5 repeats with its standard deviation. c. Record each group's masked gap: joint importance minus the sum of its members' solo importances. A positive gap is credit no single feature can claim.

For linear models abs(coef_) on standardised inputs remains acceptable, since collinearity there is visible in the coefficients themselves — but the clustering in (a) is still run and reported.

Built-in feature_importances_ (split-gain or impurity-based) may be recorded alongside as a diagnostic of how the tree was built, clearly labelled as such. It is substantially a measure of feature cardinality — in run_20260902T120000Z it ranked covid_flag last of 25 while permutation ranked it fifth — so it is never the reported importance and never the basis for a flag.

near_zero_flag is a group-level verdict: set it when a group's joint importance and its masked gap are both indistinguishable from zero. Never flag a column on its solo score — a redundant feature scores zero precisely because its twin covers for it.

10.Compute residual diagnostics for Diagnosis. On the validation set:
-Compute residuals = y_actual - y_predicted (for regression) or predicted-probability minus a threshold-based indicator (for classification).
-Save the full residuals series (with date/index column if available) to artifacts/training/iteration_<NNN>_training_val_residuals.csv.
-Compute and record: mean residual, std of residuals, and the 5th/95th percentile.
-For time-series: compute Spearman autocorrelation of residuals at lag-1 and at the seasonal lag (lag-7 for weekly, lag-12 for monthly, etc.). A high residual autocorrelation (|r| > 0.2) indicates the model is not capturing temporal structure — record this as a finding for Diagnosis.
-Compute mean residual by time period (e.g. by year or quarter) to detect systematic temporal bias — if residuals are strongly positive in early periods and negative in later ones (or vice versa), the trend or regime-change feature may be insufficient. (This kind of drift is also flagged as an operational concern in references/model_selection_timeseries.md — worth surfacing to whatever stage owns model monitoring/retraining triggers downstream of this skill, not just Diagnosis.)
-For classification: compute calibration — mean predicted probability vs observed positive rate across probability bins.
11.Record reasoning and confidence for every major decision — model family choice, hyperparameter configuration, metric selection, feature subset resolution — per conventions/naming_conventions.md. A decision left without reasoning is an unrecorded assumption that Diagnosis cannot act on.
12.Raise clarification_needed for genuine ambiguity. Same rules as all other nodes: a blocking flag, a confidence, a recommendation with its recommendation_reasoning and impact_if_wrong (field table in the Planner's Clarification Handling section), and never a self-decision to pause the workflow. Typical triggers: deployment_scenario is unspecified, metric preference is ambiguous, seasonal period for MASE is unclear, or a suspected leakage feature was found in step 1. Each of those has an obvious default this node can name — the conservative scenario, the metric EDA recommended, the period the ACF actually shows — so name it rather than presenting the question bare.
13.Record any execution failures in issues. A model that failed to converge, a metric that returned NaN, a NaN found in the feature set — record rather than silently omitting.
14.Write outputs and generate artifacts. Save:
-Model: artifacts/training/iteration_<NNN>_training_model.pkl
-Residuals: artifacts/training/iteration_<NNN>_training_val_residuals.csv
-History JSON: history/iteration_<NNN>_training.json
-Code: code/iteration_<NNN>_training.py
-Report: reports/iteration_<NNN>_training.md
-Update state/current.json: latest_model_path, latest_metrics, current_hypothesis

Minimum required artifacts (each plot paired with a CSV of the plotted values; see references/plotting_guide.md for the full condition → plot table this is the floor of, including classification-specific, iterative-model-training-curve, hyperparameter-search, interpretability, and iteration-tracking plots that apply beyond this fixed list):

-feature_importance — ranked bar chart of all features by importance
-actual_vs_predicted_val — scatter or time-series overlay of actual vs predicted on validation set
-residuals_over_time — residuals plotted in chronological order on validation set (reveals temporal bias)
-residuals_distribution — histogram of validation residuals (reveals skew, outliers)

For time-series, also generate:

-residual_acf — autocorrelation of residuals at lags 1 through at least 14 (reveals whether temporal structure remains uncaptured)
15.Generate a human-readable report. Write reports/iteration_<NNN>_training.md covering: mode and what triggered this call; feature subset used and deployment scenario; model family and hyperparameters with reasoning; train and validation metrics (primary + all secondary); MASE and its interpretation relative to the seasonal naive baseline (for time-series); overfitting assessment; top-10 feature importance ranking; residual diagnostic findings and what they imply for Diagnosis; clarification_needed entries; issues. Write explanations, not just numbers — a metric without context is not actionable.
16.Log to MLflow (required for every training call).

After all artifacts and the history JSON have been written, append the following block to the end of the generated code/iteration_<NNN>_training_*.py script. This is the last thing the script does; nothing after it can affect training results.

   # ── MLflow logging ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   import glob as _glob
   import mlflow as _mlflow
   import mlflow.lightgbm as _mlflow_lgb
   import lightgbm as _lgb

   _HERE     = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))   # code/
   _RUN_DIR  = os.path.dirname(_HERE)                       # run root
   _PROJ_DIR = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(_RUN_DIR))   # General Plan/
   _MLDB     = os.path.join(_PROJ_DIR, "mlflow.db")

   _mlflow.set_tracking_uri("sqlite:///" + _MLDB.replace("\\", "/"))
   _mlflow.set_experiment("bread_demand_forecast")

   _RUN_ID = os.path.basename(_RUN_DIR)
   _ITER   = os.path.splitext(os.path.basename(__file__))[0]  # e.g. iteration_005_training_ml_regression

   with _mlflow.start_run(run_name=f"{_RUN_ID}__{_ITER}"):
       # ── tags ──
       _mlflow.set_tags({
           "pipeline_run_id": _RUN_ID,
           "iteration_id":    _ITER,
           "mode":            MODE,            # set earlier in this script
           "model_type":      MODEL_TYPE,      # set earlier in this script (e.g. "LightGBM")
       })

       # ── params ──
       _mlflow.log_params({k: v for k, v in LGBM_PARAMS.items()
                           if isinstance(v, (int, float, str, bool))})
       _mlflow.log_param("n_features",           len(SAFE_FEATURES))
       _mlflow.log_param("early_stopping_rounds", EARLY_STOPPING_ROUNDS)

       # ── per-horizon metrics ──
       _pooled_maes = []
       for _h, _mae in VAL_MAE_BY_HORIZON.items():   # dict populated during training loop
           _mlflow.log_metric(f"val_mae_h{_h}", _mae)
           _pooled_maes.append(_mae)
       if _pooled_maes:
           _mlflow.log_metric("val_mae_pooled", sum(_pooled_maes) / len(_pooled_maes))

       # ── artifacts: plots ──
       _art_dir = os.path.join(_RUN_DIR, "artifacts", "training")
       for _png in _glob.glob(os.path.join(_art_dir, f"{_ITER}_*.png")):
           _mlflow.log_artifact(_png, artifact_path="plots")

       # ── models: LightGBM text dumps → MLflow model registry ──
       _models_dir = os.path.join(_art_dir, "models")
       for _h in HORIZONS:
           _dump = os.path.join(_models_dir, f"lgbm_h{_h}.txt")
           if os.path.exists(_dump):
               _booster = _lgb.Booster(model_file=_dump)
               _mlflow_lgb.log_model(_booster, name=f"lgbm_h{_h}")
   # ── end MLflow logging ───────────────────────────────────────────────────

Adapt the snippet to the model family being trained:

-For classical statistical (ARIMA/SARIMA): replace the LightGBM params block with the fitted orders (arima_p, arima_d, arima_q, sarima_P, sarima_D, sarima_Q, sarima_m, arima_aic, sarima_aic). Log per-horizon MAE under arima_val_mae_h{h} and sarima_val_mae_h{h}. Omit the model registration block (statsmodels ARIMA results files are logged as plain artifacts instead via mlflow.log_artifact).
-For baseline (no learned model): log only per-horizon MAE from baseline_results under val_mae_h{h}. No params or model registration.
-For any model family with a sklearn-compatible .predict(): use mlflow.sklearn.log_model() in place of the LightGBM call.

Required dict VAL_MAE_BY_HORIZON: the training loop must populate a dict[int, float] named exactly VAL_MAE_BY_HORIZON (keys = horizon integers) so the MLflow block can read it without knowledge of the loop's internals. Add VAL_MAE_BY_HORIZON: dict[int, float] = {} before the training loop and VAL_MAE_BY_HORIZON[h] = float(val_mae) inside it, immediately after computing val_mae for horizon h.

Guardrails for this step:

-The MLflow block must be the last thing the script does — never place it before a model save or a history-JSON write, so a logging failure cannot corrupt outputs.
-All paths are constructed from __file__ — never hard-code an absolute path.
-The experiment name "bread_demand_forecast" must be constant across all calls in a project so all pipeline runs land in the same MLflow experiment and can be compared side by side.
-mlflow and lightgbm must already be installed in the sandbox (they are listed under "Tools available"). Do not add pip install calls to generated training code.

Handoff block (required)

Before writing the output, add a top-level handoff block to this node's history/iteration_<NNN>_<node>.json. The field rules, the required fields, and the externalisation pass that must be run before finishing are all in conventions/handoff_contract.md — that file is the specification, and it is what tools/handoff_check.py validates against.

Two things worth restating here because they are the failures this node can actually cause:

-A finding recorded in agent_initiated_findings that changes what a later node should do must be duplicated into the handoff. The two serve different readers: one is the honest record of what was explored, the other is the instruction set for whoever runs next.
-A node that genuinely changes nothing downstream still writes the block, with empty lists and context_clearable: true. An absent block is indistinguishable from a forgotten one.

Guardrails

-Generated code is a cell-marked .py, and every plot names itself (conventions/code_and_plot_conventions.md). Scripts carry # %% markers so the same file stays diffable and converts to a notebook on demand — never write a .ipynb as the artifact. Every figure carries its declared name as the title, its declared type stated in the figure, and its iteration - node provenance, using the same strings recorded in the JSON. A plot that is unidentifiable once separated from its report is not finished.
-Never end a call without a handoff block (conventions/handoff_contract.md). Context may be cleared immediately after this node returns; anything load-bearing that exists only in prose, only in a code file, or only in agent_initiated_findings is lost at that point. Never store a count where a later node needs the content.
-There are no held-out rows in this dataset to protect. The genuinely held-out set was removed before the run began and is scored outside this pipeline. What must be protected here is the validation partition: it is the only ranking signal the run has, and it is reused on every iteration, so treat it the way a test set would be treated within a single call — fit nothing on it, tune nothing directly against a single reading of it, and prefer the cross-validated estimate where split_info.cv_design provides one.
-Never use random cross-validation (random k-fold, stratified k-fold) for time-series data. Random folds allow future rows to appear in training folds and past rows in validation folds, leaking temporal structure. Always use TimeSeriesSplit or the fixed chronological split. See references/cross_validation.md for the full CV-strategy decision table and the reasoning behind it.
-Never fit any statistic on validation rows — including scaling, imputation, or any preprocessing applied inside the training loop. All such statistics must come from Preprocess (already fit on train) or from training rows only within this node. (Same rule references/ cross_validation.md §3 states generally: fit on training folds only, apply to validation.)
-Never impute, scale, or encode features here — that is Preprocess's job. If the feature set has NaN values or unencoded categoricals, record an issues entry and request a Preprocess fix rather than silently patching it in the training loop. Model-specific scaling/encoding/ NaN-handling requirements that inform what to ask Preprocess for are documented in ../shared-references/preprocessing_and_feature_engineering.md (e.g. §6 explains why LightGBM's native NaN handling matters for the step 2b decision table).
-Never treat model training as a substitute for feature selection — high feature importance does not retroactively justify a feature that failed the FE variance-in-train or relevance checks. Low feature importance on a kept feature is a signal for Diagnosis to act on, not an error.
-Never report a per-feature importance ranking as the top-level answer, and never set near_zero_flag from a column's solo score. Both are the identifiability failure that ../shared-references/feature_attribution.md exists to prevent: under correlation, a per-feature number describes which twin the fit reached first, not what the model depends on.
-Never present any number this node produces as final performance. Every metric here is a validation metric and must be labelled as one. The unbiased held-out score is produced after the pipeline finishes, against data this run never had.
-Respect the selection-noise band. Where split_info.selection_noise_band is set, a difference smaller than it is a tie, not an improvement — say so rather than ranking on it. This run is expected to compare many candidates, and without this guard the winner is partly whichever model happened to suit one validation draw.
-For MASE: always compute the denominator on training data only. Using the full dataset to compute the naive baseline denominator would let future demand levels influence what counts as a "good" score on past data.
-Every artifact plot must have a paired CSV. Never load that CSV into your own reasoning context.
-Every decision — model family, hyperparameter, metric choice — needs reasoning and confidence. A decision recorded only as "default" is an unrecorded assumption.
-The reports/ Markdown file must only restate what is already in the JSON output.
-Never train one model for several horizons. Each active horizon gets its own fit, its own feature subset, its own target column and its own artifact. A metric pooled across horizons is never reported without the per-horizon table beside it.
-Never use target_horizons on a baseline call. The floor must be established for every horizon in forecast_horizons at once — a horizon missing a baseline cannot be stopped against.
-Never use a feature whose min_horizon exceeds the horizon being trained. A lag-1 feature in a 30-day-ahead model is not a feature, it is a value nobody will have at prediction time — the same failure as a concurrent feature in a live forecast, one lead time further out.
-Never use a feature whose known_future_horizon is below the horizon being trained, and never substitute its origin value instead. This is the reciprocal bound and the one more easily missed, because nothing about the stale value looks wrong: origin weather at h = 90 is a well-formed number that carries no information about the target, and a model handed it will spend capacity on noise. Drop the feature for that horizon. Read evaluated_at and honour it: a feature marked target_date is joined on the target date, not the origin, and reading it at the wrong anchor silently changes what the column means.
-Never drop, prune, or exclude a column listed in context.protected_features from the horizon it belongs to. Not for redundancy, not for near-zero importance, not for a >0.98 correlation with the target — that correlation is the feature working. Evidence against one is raised as a blocking clarification and answered by the user, never acted on here.
-Never feed a naive predictor to a horizon other than its own. naive_h7_* is computed at origin target − 7; in the h = 30 model it reads the series 23 periods after that model's origin. The resulting model scores better on validation and worse on the holdout, which is the hardest failure in this pipeline to detect after the fact.
-Take horizon_feature_subsets as given; never re-derive it here. If a horizon's subset looks wrong, that is a finding routed back to Feature Engineering, not something to patch in the training loop — two nodes deciding the same thing is how they drift apart.
-Default hyperparameters are a starting point, never the run's final answer. Fitting on library defaults for a first pass is correct and cheap. Closing the run without a single search is not: it leaves the largest cheap axis unmeasured, and tools/stop_check.py blocks the stop for exactly this reason. "Re-tuning would invalidate the baseline comparison" is not a reason — a baseline is a fixed reference and does not move when a model is tuned. Where a search is genuinely inadvisable (too few rows, a validation window too small to select on), say so in hyperparameter_search.reasoning with the row count that makes it so, rather than leaving the field null and the axis silently closed.
-Never report a time-series iteration without all four of MAE, RMSE, SMAPE and MASE, on train and validation both, whichever one is primary. Choosing the primary is the agent's call; computing the other three is not optional. Where they disagree on the ranking, say so.
-Never let a time-series run consist only of ML-as-regression fits. Both non-automatic approaches in references/model_selection_timeseries.md §1 must be fitted at least once, on the same validation rows and the same primary metric. This node does not choose when — the Planner routes — but it does report the gap (ts_approach_gap) every call until it is closed.
-Never close the classical slot without an ARIMA-family fit. ARIMA, SARIMA, or SARIMAX — exponential smoothing alone does not close it, and neither does an Auto ARIMA run whose orders were never recorded. Where the series' structure sends the choice to SARIMA/SARIMAX, plain ARIMA is still fitted once as the ablation that prices the seasonal terms.
-Never decide on your own to pause the workflow — raise clarification_needed and let the Planner decide.

Input / output contract

Full input/output example: contracts/training.json.

On a multi-horizon task every model-specific section below is recorded per horizon, keyed by horizon — trained_model_path, model_family, model_class, hyperparameters, feature_subset_used, metrics, feature_importance, residuals_summary, vs_baseline_floor — alongside horizons_trained_this_call (the active set for this call) and horizons_skipped_this_call (horizons in forecast_horizons not touched this call — empty list when target_horizons was absent). Sections that are genuinely shared (deployment_scenario, the primary metric choice) stay single and say so.

Top-level output sections: schema_version, trained_model_path, model_family, model_class, model_selection_reasoning (which decision-table rows fired and why — or override source if step 2a applied), ts_approach (time-series calls only: classical_statistical, ml_as_regression, or automatic — step 2b-ts), ts_approach_gap (the non-automatic approach the run has still never fitted, or null), feature_subset_used, feature_subset_type (concurrent_included or pre_period_only), deployment_scenario, hyperparameters (each with value and reasoning), hyperparameter_search (method, n_trials, search_space — null if defaults used), training_summary (n_train_rows, n_val_rows, n_features, training_time_seconds, target_transform — the transform applied to the target column, or null if none), metrics (train and validation objects, each with all computed metrics; for time-series always include mae, rmse and smape — the last with its zero-handling convention and the affected row count — alongside mase with seasonal_period, naive_baseline_mae_train, and mase_value, regardless of which is primary), naive_predictor_features (present when mode == "baseline": the per-horizon predictor specs from baseline-skill/baseline.md Part B, with the search grid, the deduplication result and selection_basis: "train_rows_only"), baseline_floor (present when mode == "baseline": baseline_type, the rule or seasonal period, the full metric set pooled and per segment/horizon), vs_baseline_floor (every other call: margin per segment and per horizon, and whether the model beats the floor everywhere or only pooled), baseline_model (present when mode == "initial"; contains baseline_type, train_<primary_metric>, val_<primary_metric>, and vs_primary_model assessment: one of primary_better, primary_worse — flag as finding if primary_worse; null in incremental/ rebuild mode unless Diagnosis requested a re-comparison), overfitting_check (ratio, assessment string), feature_importance (groups: ranked list, each entry: group_name, members, importance, importance_sd, sum_solo, masked, rank, near_zero_flag; per_feature: solo permutation value per column, reported only inside its group; builtin_importance: optional, labelled as a build diagnostic — see ../shared-references/feature_attribution.md), residuals_summary (val_residuals_path, mean, std, p5, p95; for time-series: acf_lag1, acf_seasonal_lag, temporal_bias_by_period), clarification_needed, agent_initiated_findings, issues, artifact_paths (plots list, each with path and data_path).

Comparison: Databricks Genie Code

  Databricks Genie Codeas Databricks describes it This pipelinewhat the design chose instead
When it plansLive, at request timeIn development.
Context costPersistent memory that grows run over runDisposable. Clear the history at any step and the next one resumes from disk
Reproducing a runThrough the platform that produced itDeployable to any platform
Which answers Did the agent finish the job? Is the model it produced any good?

  },

  "history": [ one entry per completed skill: 16 in state, 29 on disk ]
}
Every skill reads this file and writes back to it. The Planner reasons over nothing else : no shared memory, no conversation history, just the state and the handoff block it wrote last iteration.

The 64 features, and why the agent built each one

Naive anchors18 featuresΔMAE +3.37
The Baseline skill tested 22 zero-parameter rules and kept the three best windows per horizon, then handed their forecasts to the model as ordinary columns. Four of the six champions do not predict demand at all. They predict a ratio to one of these anchors, which is why the block is worth more than everything else combined.

Calendar17 featuresΔMAE +1.16
Plain date parts plus the Belgian and Flemish calendars from Domain Research. The agent dropped five of these at iteration 5 for failing a Spearman relevance test, then put them back at iteration 19 when it went looking for unused domain evidence. On the holdout the block is worth +1.16, so re-adding them was right, and the relevance test was wrong.

Lags8 featuresΔMAE +0.43
The strongest correlations in the set. Critically, each lag is resolved by calendar date — date_to_val[d − timedelta(days=L)] , not by row offset, and the windows are ceil(h/7) × 7 so every horizon uses a lag it could actually have known. An earlier run measured autocorrelation in row offsets on a frame with Mondays deleted, where a week is six rows, and built an aliased ladder. This one did not.

bread_lag_14d0.700two weeks. Causal for h ≤ 14

bread_lag_91d0.648thirteen weeks, the h=90 lag
bread_lag_1d0.395yesterday. Added at iter 19; 0.14 of the gain at t+90

bread_lag_3d0.056three days back
Weather13 featuresΔMAE −0.22
EDA asked for temperature, precipitation and wind. The agent took the whole block and added four derived columns. The source starts in 2015, so these are blank for the first five years of training, which is what weather_data_available really encodes, and why it correlates at −0.43: it is a proxy for "before 2015", not for weather. The only group that made the holdout worse.

Competitor4 featuresΔMAE 0.00
Leave and holiday flags for five nearby bakeries, on the theory that a rival closing sends customers here. The source runs 2017-07 to 2020-09-15 and then stops. So across the entire 2021 holdout all four columns are constant zero . The block carries 0.06 of the model gain at t+1 and is structurally incapable of contributing anything where it is scored.
FeaturerWhy
comp_n_competitors_closed−0.089how many of the five are shut that day
comp_any_closed−0.090any of them shut at all
comp_closure_density−0.089rolling share of recent days with a closure
comp_data_available−0.256a coverage flag. Like the weather one, it encodes the era
Regime3 featuresΔMAE 0.00
The three structural breaks declared in protocol.json. All are constant or near-constant in 2021, so like the competitor block they cannot move the holdout metric, but they do stop the model reading the 2014 gap and the pre-2020 Monday closures as demand signal during training.
FeaturerWhy
is_closed_monday—Mondays before 2020-06-01. Zero variance in the 2021 holdout
regime_x_monday−0.063the interaction: Monday after the 7/7 switch
is_2014_sparse_period0.059the year where only 64 of ~310 trading days survive
Trend1 featureΔMAE 0.00
A monotonic term for the falling level, and the clearest single lesson in this appendix. It carries 0.08 of the gain at t+60 and 0.11 at t+90, so the model plainly uses it. But it runs 0 to 9.6 in training and 10.1 to 11.1 on the holdout: every test value sits past the last split the tree ever learned, so it always routes the same way. A gradient-boosted tree cannot extrapolate, and this is what that costs: nothing gained, and the level bias left unfixed.
FeaturerWhy
year_trend−0.395years since 2010-11-16, as a float
Dropped9 columnsnever modelled
Eight of these are same-day operational totals from the till: knowing the day's revenue tells you the day's bread. The agent refused them all as leakage at iteration 5, before fitting anything.
ColumnrWhy
total_quantity—leakage: concurrent same-day operational metric
total_revenue—leakage: concurrent same-day operational metric
bread_revenue—leakage: the target in euros
pistolet_quantity—leakage: a sibling product line, same day
num_orders—leakage: same-day footfall
payment_mode_1—leakage: same-day transaction mix
payment_mode_2—leakage: same-day transaction mix
payment_mode_4—leakage: same-day transaction mix
had_reduction—near-constant: 99.9% of rows carry the same value
r is Spearman correlation against bread sold on the same day, measured on the 2,713 fold-3 training rows, the run's own convention. It reproduces the values recorded in iteration_005_feature_engineering.json exactly, and it is a training-set diagnostic, not holdout evidence.
ΔMAE is grouped permutation importance on the 2021 holdout, averaged over the six horizons, 5 shuffles each: positive means removing the group made the model worse, negative means removing it made the model better. Three groups score exactly 0.00 because their columns are constant across the holdout, so shuffling them changes nothing.
